title: Philosophy of language
audience: a college student in a philosophy degree program, or an adult studying the same material on their own
purpose: Study meaning and reference: Frege on sense and reference, Russell on definite descriptions, Kripke on names and necessity, rigid designation and the necessary a posteriori, natural kind terms and externalism, theories of truth and truth-conditional semantics, speech acts and implicature, and context, indexicals and vagueness.
primary_reading: MIT OpenCourseWare 24.251 Introduction to Philosophy of Language (free)

weeks.3: Russell: definite descriptions and negative existentials
weeks.5: Kripke: names and the modal argument
weeks.6: Rigid designation and the necessary a posteriori
weeks.7: The causal theory of reference and natural kind terms
weeks.8: Twin Earth and externalism about meaning

blocks.deliverable: Explain Frege's puzzle with two new examples.
Analyze four sentences with Russell's theory.
Reconstruct the modal argument against descriptivism.
Week 7 midterm; explain the Twin Earth argument.
State Tarski's convention T and give instances.
Explain one implicature and one context-sensitive term.
Submit the project; take an unseen 120 minute final in week 14.

project: Philosophy of language paper: write a 2,500-word paper on how a theory of names or descriptions bears on a metaphysical question (negative existentials, the necessary a posteriori, or names in fiction), reconstructing the main arguments and defending a view.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
